Order:

(per the Hon'ble Sri Justice P.SAM KOSHY) Heard Ms. R. Sowmya Reddy, learned counsel,
appearing on behalf of Mr. Pasham Trivikram Reddy, learned counsel for the petitioner and Mr.
Swaroop Oorilla, learned Special Government Pleader, representing learned Additional Advocate General, for the respondents.
2.

The instant is a writ petition which has been filed challenging the order dated 26.08.2024 (Annexure P-1) passed by respondent No.2 putting detenu under preventive detention under Sub-Section (2) of Section 3 of the "The Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Bootleggers, Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders, Land-Grabbers,
Spurious Seed Offenders, Insecticide Offenders, Fertiliser Offenders, Food Adulteration Offenders,
Fake Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Offenders, Gaming Offenders,
Sexual Offenders, Explosive Substances Offenders, Arms Offenders, Cyber Crime Offenders and White Collar or Financial Offenders Act, 1986 (for short, 'the Act of 1986').
3.

entities.text: Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Bootleggers, Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The writ petition is one which has been filed seeking for issuance of a Writ in the nature of Habeas Corpus with prayer for production of the detenu before the Court and quashment of the aforementioned orders.

4. The brief facts of the case are that the detenu has committed an offence under clause (f) of Section 2 of the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986, across various Police Station limits but the police authorities had detained the detenu on 26.08.2024 under multiple cases during the period between 2023 and 2024 where the detenu was involved in NDPS Act and engaged in illegal and highly dangerous activities of peddling Contraband Cannabis / Ganja among the innocent which was registered within the jurisdiction of Warangal Police Commissionerate indicating a pattern of persistent and organized drug trafficking.

entities.text: Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The authorities have expressed grave concern over the impact of detenu's actions endangering the lives of people especially youth causing irreparable damages to their central nervous system and thereby crippling the mental and physical health of the people.
The detenu was arrested on 08.06.2024 in Cr.No.81 of 2024 for the offences under Section 20 (b) (ii) (C) of NDPS Act.

The detenu's criminal history reveals a pattern of organized drug trafficking where the detenu would purchase ganja at lower rates from Andhra Pradesh, transport it to Maharashtra and other locations and sell it at higher prices while evading S. sentences.text:
The detenu had been previously involved in four NDPS Act cases i.e. Cr.No.115 of 2004 at PS Parkal, Cr.No.96 of 2020 at PS Regonda where 22.782 Kgs of ganja worth Rs.
1,13,000/- was seized, Cr.No.165 of 2021 at PS Enkur where 70 Kgs worth Rs. 3,50,000/- was recovered, and Cr.No.160 of 2023 at PS KUC Hanamkonda involving 2.1 Kgs worth Rs. 1,05,000/-.
Despite being remanded to judicial custody multiple times, the detenu carried on his illegal activities.

5. The authorities determined that ordinary law was insufficient to curb his unlawful activities as evidenced by his continued involvement in drug trafficking despite multiple arrests and incarcerations.
The detenu had made multiple attempts to secure bail in his recent case (Cr.No.81 of 2024) with two bail petitions already being dismissed.

However, considering the possibility of future bail applications and potential release and given his extensive network and use of technology to evade police surveillance, it was deemed necessary to issue a detention order.
The order, dated 26.08.2024, directed his detention in Central Prison, Cherlapalli, to prevent further drug-related activities that could harm public health and order.

6. Thus, the impugned order was challenged on the grounds that these alleged crimes fall under the purview of ordinary law and do not constitute a disturbance of public order, questioning the necessity and legality of the detention order under the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act.

entities.text: Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 7. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the detention order was passed while the detenu was already in judicial custody and the apprehension of the detenu coming out of prison and committing similar offenses is misplaced which represent an abuse of executive power.

Further, the learned counsel for the petitioner contended the authority concerned had wrongly invoked this draconian law for a case that clearly falls under ordinary criminal law jurisdiction and erroneously treated a law and order issue as a public order concern.
8. The learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the detention order was passed mechanically without proper application of mind, based on vague, stale, and irrelevant grounds.
It was contended that the classification of the detenu as a "Drug Offender" under section 2(f) of the Act is entirely unsupported by material evidence.
The authorities have failed to present any substantial proof or documentation to justify this classification making the detention order arbitrary and unjustified.
The use of preventive detention law in this case violates established legal principles as regular criminal proceedings would have been more appropriate and sufficient to address the alleged offenses.
9. Lastly, the learned counsel for the petitioner argued that the detention order gravely violates fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 21 and 22 of the Constitution of India.

The persistent refusal of the authority concerned to file counter affidavit without confirmation orders and their insistence on challenging consequential orders clearly demonstrates a systematic abuse of process and deliberately prolonging illegal detention.

sentences.text:
The learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the recent Supreme Court judgments,
particularly Mallada K Sri Ram vs. The State of Telangana and Ors. 1, which emphasizes the exceptional nature of preventive detention and its limited application.

entities.text: Mallada K Sri Ram vs. The State of Telangana and Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Further, the learned counsel highlighted that the Supreme Court has repeatedly cautioned against the casual use of preventive detention and has stressed that deprivation of liberty even for a single day is one day too many.
Thus, the learned counsel for the petitioner prayed that the impugned order of preventive detention be set-aside and the detenu be set free.

11. Per contra, the learned Special Government Pleader argued that the detenu as a persistent drug offender has been involved in ganja peddling since 2004 operating a sophisticated network between Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra.

The learned Special Government Pleader emphasized that the detenu's activities pose a severe threat to public health, particularly endangering youth by causing irreparable damage to body organs and central nervous system.

The detenu used well-planned operational methods such as use of cell phones and technology to evade police surveillance and despite multiple arrests, the detenu showed no sign of reform, as evident from his recent arrest on 08.06.2024 when he was caught with a substantial quantity of 190 Kgs of dry ganja.

Further, the learned Special Government Pleader contended that regular law enforcement measures have proven insufficient to curb these dangerous activities noting particular concern about the possibility of bail and subsequent release which could lead to the continuation of his harmful activities affecting public order and health.

The detention order was deemed necessary due to his extensive network, persistent criminal behavior and the significant threat to society, especially considering his previous history of moving between States for drug trafficking operations and his demonstrated ability to continue operations despite previous legal interventions.
Thus, the learned Special Government Pleader prayed for dismissal of the writ petition.

13. Having heard the contentions put forth on either side and on perusal of records, it would be relevant at this juncture to refer to a recent decision of this Court itself in Writ Petition No.12085 of 2024 decided on 09.07.2024 wherein this Court dealing with similar situation had referred to a catena of decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court i.e. in Mallada K Sri Ram (supra), Nenavath Bujji Etc. vs. The State of Telangana and Ors.2, Shaik Nazeen vs. State of Telangana 3, Ram Manohar Lohia vs. State of Bihar4, Kanu Biswas vs. State of West 2024 SCC Online SC 367 (2023) 9 SCC 633 1965 SCC Online SC 9 Bengal 5, Khaja Bilal Ahmed vs. State of Telangana 6 and Ameena Begum vs.
The State of Telangana 7 and held as under, viz., "Under the given legal dictum in a series of decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court referred to in the preceding paragraphs, we have no hesitation in reaching to the conclusion that in the instant case also only because the detenu has been charged with similar type of offences in an around sixteen cases in a span of around three years by itself cannot be said to be actions which can be brought under the purview of the detention "acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of the public order".

sentences.text: Keeping in view the aforesaid statutory provisions, particularly the Act of 1986 and the details which are reproduced in the preceding paragraphs, we may now refer to a recent decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Nenavath Bujji (supra).
In the said judgment, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in paragraph Nos.23, 24 and 25 dealing with the explanation attached to Section 2(a) has held as under, viz., "23.

The explanation attached to Section 2(a) of the Act 1986 reproduced above contemplates that 'public order' shall be deemed to have been affected adversely or shall be deemed likely to be affected adversely, inter alia if any of the activities of any person referred to in Section 2(a) directly (1972) 3 SCC 831 (2020) 13 SCC 632 (2023) 9 SCC 587 or indirectly, are causing or is likely to cause any harm, danger or alarm or feeling of insecurity among the general public or any section thereof or a grave or widespread danger to life, property or public health.

The Explanation to Section 2(a) also provides that for the purpose of Section 2, a person shall be deemed to be "acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order" when such person is a "GOONDA" and engaged in activities which affect adversely or are likely to affect adversely the maintenance of public order.

It, therefore, becomes necessary to determine whether besides the person being a "GOONDA" his alleged activities are such which adversely affected the public order or are likely to affect the maintenance of public order.
24. The essential concept of preventive detention is that the detention of a person is not to punish him for something he has done but to prevent him from doing it.

The basis of detention is the satisfaction of the executive about the likelihood of the detenu acting in a manner,similar to his past acts, which is likely to affect adversely the maintenance of public order and, thereby prevent him, by an order of detention, from doing the same.
A criminal conviction on the other hand is for an act already done which can only be possible by a trial and legal evidence.
There is no parallel between the prosecution in a Court of law and a detention order under the Act 1986.
One is a punitive action and the other is a preventive act.

In one case a person is punished on proof of his guilt, and the standard is proof beyond the reasonable doubt, whereas in the other a person is detained with a view to prevent him from doing such act(s) as may be specified in the Act authorizing preventive detention.
25.
The power of preventive detention is qualitatively different from punitive detention.
The power of preventive detention is a precautionary power exercised in reasonable anticipation.
It may or may not relate to an offence.
It is not a parallel proceeding.
It does not overlap with prosecution even if it relies on certain facts for which prosecution may be launched or may have been launched.
An order of preventive detention, may be made before or during prosecution.
An order of preventive detention may be made with or without prosecution and in anticipation or after discharge or even acquittal.
The pendency of prosecution is no bar to an order of preventive detention.
An order of preventive detention is also not a bar to prosecution.

(See :HaradhanSaha v. The State of W.B., 1974 Cri LJ 1479]"
15.

entities.text: HaradhanSaha v. The State of W.B., 1974 Cri LJ 1479
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Again in paragraph No.32 of the above judgment, the Supreme Court has in great detail dealt with the expression law and order and public order and held as under,
viz., "32.
The crucial issue is whether the activities of the detenu were prejudicial to public order.

While the expression 'law and order' is wider in scope inasmuch as contravention of law always affects order, 'Public order' has a narrower ambit, and S. Manisha, vs The State Of Telangana, on 21 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59758079/
4 could be affected by only such contravention, which affects the community or the public at large.

entities.text: S. Manisha, vs The State Of Telangana
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Public order is the even tempo of life of the community taking the country as a whole or even a specified locality.
The distinction between the areas of 'law and order' and 'public order' is one of degree and extent of the reach, of the act in question on society.
It is the potentiality of the act to disturb the even tempo of life of the community which makes it prejudicial to the maintenance of the public order.
If a contravention in its effect is confined only to a few individuals directly involved as distinct from a wide spectrum of public, it could raise problem of law and order only.
In other words, the true distinction between the areas of law and order and public order lies not merely in the nature or quality of the act, but in the degree and extent of its reach upon society.
Acts similar in nature, but committed in different contexts and circumstances, might cause different reactions.

In one case it might affect specific individuals only, and therefore touches the problem of law and order only,
while in another it might affect public order.
The act by itself, therefore, is not determinant of its own gravity.

In its quality it may not differ from other similar acts,
but in its potentiality, that is, in its impact on society, it may be very different.

[See:
Union of India v. Amrit Lal Manchanda, (2004) 3 SCC 75.]"

entities.text: Union of India v. Amrit Lal Manchanda, (2004) 3 SCC 75
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 16. In yet another land mark decision in Ameena Begum (supra), a judgment which has been pronounced under the same provision of law, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held at paragraph Nos.34 to 37 as under, viz., "34.

In Kuso Sah vs. The State of Bihar, Hon'ble Y.V. Chandrachud, J. (as the Chief Justice then was) speaking for the Bench held that:
"4.*** The two concepts have well defined contours, it being well established that stray and un-organised crimes of theft and assault are not matters of public order since they do not tend to affect the even flow of public life.

entities.text: Kuso Sah vs. The State of Bihar
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Infractions of law are bound in some measure to lead to disorder but every infraction of law does not necessarily result in public disorder.

* * The power to detain a person without the safeguard of a court trial is too drastic to permit a lenient construction and therefore Courts must be astute to ensure that the detaining authority does not transgress the limitations subject to which alone the power can be exercised.

** *" 
(underlining ours, for emphasis)

35. Turning our attention to section 3(1) of the Act, the Government has to arrive at a subjective satisfaction that a goonda (as in the present case) has to be detained, in order to prevent him from acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order.
Therefore, we first direct ourselves to the examination of what constitutes 'public order'.
Even within the provisions of the Act, the term "public order" has, strictosensu, been defined in narrow and restricted terms.
An order of detention under section 3(1) of the Act can only be issued against a detenu to prevent him "from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order".

"Public order"

5 is defined in the Explanation to section 2(a) of the Act as encompassing situations that cause "harm, danger or alarm or a feeling of insecurity among the general public or any section thereof or a grave wide-spread danger to life or public health".

entities.text: S. Manisha, vs The State Of Telangana
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
36. Ram Manohar Lohia (supra) is an authority to rely upon for the proposition that if liberty of an individual can be invaded under statutory rules by the simple process of making of a certain order,
he can be so deprived only if the order is in consonance with the said rule. Strict compliance with the letter of the rule, in such a case, has to be the essence of the matter since the statute has the potentiality to interfere with the personal liberty of an individual and a Court is precluded from going behind its face.
Though circumstances may make it necessary for ordering a detention without trial, but it would be perfectly legitimate to require strict observance of the rules in such cases.
If there is any doubt whether the rules have been strictly observed, that doubt must be resolved in favour of the detenu.
37. Rekha too (supra) provides a useful guide.

It is said in paragraph 30 that:
"30. Whenever an order under a preventive detention law is challenged one of the questions the court must ask in deciding its legality is: was the ordinary law of the land sufficient to deal with the situation?
If the answer is in the affirmative, the detention order will be illegal.
In the present case, the charge against the detenu was of selling expired drugs after changing their labels.
Surely the relevant provisions in the Penal Code and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act were sufficient to deal with this situation.
Hence, in our opinion, for this reason also the detention order in question was illegal."

17. Under the given legal dictum in a series of decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court referred to in the preceding paragraphs, we have no hesitation in reaching to the conclusion that the preventive detention order lacks substantial justification and is arbitrary in nature.

We find that the detention order appears to be primarily based on speculative assumptions regarding the detenu's potential future involvement in criminal activities rather than a concrete evidence or reasonable grounds.
Such preventive detention orders cannot be sustained merely on the basis of anticipation or presumptive criminal conduct.
The fundamental principles of natural justice and personal liberty ensure that preventive detention must be based on credible material and reasonable probability and not on mere suspicion.

18. Further, a particularly troubling aspect of this case is the failure of the detaining authority to demonstrate the existence of a real and imminent threat to public order or security that would justify such a severe restriction of personal liberty.
We find that there is an administrative overreach where the extraordinary power of preventive detention has been exercised without adequate justification.
It is pertinent to note that preventive detention is an exceptional measure that should be used sparingly and only when alternative remedies is insufficient to address the situation.
This not only threatens individual liberty but also risks eroding public trust in the fairness and impartiality of the legal system.

sentences.text: Furthermore, we note with concern that the detention order fails to meet the established legal standards of reasonableness and proportionality.
These principles require that any restriction on fundamental rights must be proportionate and the least restrictive means to achieve the legitimate aim.
In the present case, the authorities have failed to demonstrate how these essential requirements have been met.
The preventive detention order appears to have been passed without due regard to the exceptional nature of preventive detention and its serious implications on individual liberty.

20. Hence, upon careful consideration of the matter before us, we find that the reasoning provided by the authorities concerned in passing the impugned order of preventive detention lacks sufficient justification and fails to meet the requisite legal standards.
The preventive detention order is thus unsustainable in law and becomes difficult to uphold the same.
As a consequence, the impugned order of preventive detention dated 26.08.2024 and also the orders passed by the Advisory Board are liable to be set-aside / quashed and it is ordered accordingly.
The writ petition accordingly stands allowed.
If the detenu is otherwise not wanted in any other case, he may be released from the detention forthwith.
No costs.
21. As a sequel, miscellaneous petitions pending if any, shall stand closed.
